section: Educational Psychology · Ch13 — Types of Validity (Complete)
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: Researchers designing a new 'creativity test' check whether scores align with the theoretical characteristics creativity is expected to have (e.g. correlating with divergent thinking tasks but not with rote memory tests). This process of checking whether a test truly measures its underlying theoretical concept is called establishing:
explanation: Construct validity concerns whether a test genuinely measures the theoretical construct (e.g. creativity, intelligence) it claims to, verified by checking relationships with other variables theory predicts — distinct from content validity, which concerns coverage of a defined syllabus/domain.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch13 — Types of Validity (Complete)
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: An entrance exam's scores are checked against students' actual academic performance two years later, to see if high scorers indeed go on to perform well. This is an example of establishing:
explanation: Predictive validity is a type of criterion-related validity established by correlating test scores with a FUTURE outcome/criterion — here, performance two years later. Concurrent validity instead correlates with a criterion measured at roughly the SAME time.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch13 — Types of Validity (Complete)
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A newly designed short screening test for reading difficulty is administered to students, and its scores are compared, in the same week, with an already-established, lengthier diagnostic reading test. This comparison establishes:
explanation: Concurrent validity is established by correlating a new test's scores with an already-validated measure taken around the SAME time — useful for validating shorter/quicker alternatives to established, lengthier tests.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch13 — Types of Validity (Complete)
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A parent looks at a maths test paper and remarks, 'this certainly looks like a proper maths test' — based purely on its superficial appearance, without any statistical analysis. This is the weakest, most subjective form of validity, called:
explanation: Face validity is merely whether a test APPEARS, on the surface, to measure what it claims — a subjective, non-statistical judgment, and the weakest form of validity evidence compared to content, construct, or criterion-related validity.
